newsitem.title: GERMANY: Strong state must bring order to economy - Lebed.
newsitem.headline: Strong state must bring order to economy - Lebed.

text.p: Russian presidential hopeful Alexander Lebed called for a strong state to regulate prices of essential consumer goods and take control of foreign trade as a way of restoring order to a chaotic economy.

In an address to an invited audience in Bonn late on Wednesday, Lebed also praised the success of southeast Asian states in developing industry on the basis of their own models rather than International Money Fund (IMF) guidelines.

Lebed, a retired general whom polls show to be the most popular politician in Russia, is on a five-day visit to Germany to introduce himself to the establishment as a possible future successor to ailing President Boris Yeltsin.
Despite coming a strong third in last year's election, Lebed has so far given few hints about his economic priorities.

"I know that if serious business is to be done in Russia, then there must be elementary order," Lebed said. He added that the success of a business must depend on rigidly enforced rules and not on how well an entrepreneur gets on with those in power.
"The state must be strong enough to ensure the application of rules which are normal business practice in all civilised countries," he said.
Lebed praised the rapidly growing economies of southeast Asia, saying that "those countries created the foundations for economic success on the basis of their own models, not the advice of the IMF".
He said the Russian government should take control of pricing of the most essential consumer goods, adding that state regulation had been the basis of early post-war reconstruction in western Europe.
And he called for the state to take temporary control of certain sectors of foreign trade to boost its revenues.
"We need to designate those areas of foreign trade which can quickly bring in significant funds for state coffers.

"For a clearly defined period of time -- and I emphasise, for a clearly defined period -- we must set up a state monopoly in those areas, while guaranteeing the property rights of the non-state parties taking part in economic activity."
Lebed said he would impose tougher measures to clamp down on Russia's flourishing dollar economy and ensure all business was done in roubles.
He called for a climate to be created that encouraged private investment and the establishment of a middle class as the best guarantee against social upheaval.
And he said he would introduce a range of measures to make Russia more predictable and attractive for foreign investors and remove obstacles to capital inflow.
"It shouldn't be asking too much to change customs rules no more than once a year...and to give at least three months' notice," he said.

Lebed also called for a reform of the tax system and said he would slash Russia's bureaucracy, which he said had mushroomed to 22 million people in a country of 174 million from just 18 million in the pre-1991 Soviet Union -- which had a population of over 270 million.
